transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2028-10-31
Start: 15:00 PT
Duration: 46m
Attendees: Jordan Miles (Redwood AE), Priya Natarajan (Redwood SE), Carlos Ruiz (CTO - Arkhaven), Maya Chen (ML Infra), Liam O'Neill (SRE), Sofia Park (Product)

Summary (auto): High-level latency and hosting-mode tradeoff discussion. Agreement to run pilot benchmarks. Requested security docs and benchmark harness.

Topics: p95 targets, streaming vs non-streaming, batching/caching, dedicated capacity sizing, VPC/private connectivity, SOC2 + KMS, sample prompt sets, timeline for pilot.

Transcript body:
[00:00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone thanks for joining on a Tuesday afternoon, uh quick intros — I'm Jordan Miles AE at Redwood, and with me is Priya on SE side.
[00:00:12] Carlos: Hey team, Carlos here, CTO at Arkhaven. We're mainly interested in how Redwood handles streaming assistant use cases at p95 under load.
[00:00:20] Priya: Great, thanks Carlos. Can you kick off with current architecture and what you're seeing today?
[00:00:28] Carlos: Yeah so quick thing, our stack is a mix — front end in node, API layer on our K8s cluster in GCP, we have an internal model orchestrator right now that talks to a mixture of cloud vendor endpoints and a self-hosted Llama variant. Latency is all over the place, p95s spike during morning batch jobs, and we get token floods.
[00:00:48] Maya: To add, typical request is short-form assistant answers, about 30-80 tokens, but we have a long tail where some requests go 800-1,200 tokens. For streaming chat we care about initial token latency — waterfall of token streaming.
[00:01:05] Liam: And ops wants predictable tail latencies, not just averages. Our SLO is basically 99% under 1s, but p95 target for the product team is 200-300ms for the initial streaming chunk.
[00:01:20] Jordan: That's helpful — so when you say initial streaming chunk, are you expecting streaming delta within 200ms or full response?
[00:01:28] Sofia: Initial chunk, we want the assistant to start responding super fast to feel real-time. Full completion can be slower but initial token must be snappy.
[00:01:37] Priya: Excellent. On Redwood side, there are a few levers — hosting mode (Hosted API vs Dedicated reserved capacity vs Private VPC/on-prem), batching and continuous batching, prefix/KV cache, and pipelined streaming. Each has different latency/cost tradeoffs.
[00:01:55] Carlos: Can you speak to concrete numbers? If we need 200ms p95 for initial token at 1.5k concurrent streaming sessions, is that feasible hosted?
[00:02:06] Priya: Short answer: maybe. Longer answer depends on sequence length, model size, whether you can accept a quantized variant, and whether prefix caching covers a lot of your prompts. Hosted can hit low p95s, but at high concurrency you may need Dedicated to avoid noisy neighbors and guarantee throughput. For 1.5k concurrent streams we typically suggest a Dedicated pool or a hosted burst+reserved hybrid.
[00:02:30] Jordan: Also routing matters — smart routing to cheaper variants for non-critical traffic, and fallback to a smaller model for bursts. But for primary UX you probably want Dedicated or Private to pin capacity.
[00:02:44] Maya: Our security team mandates KMS-backed key management and audit logs. We also need SSO/SAML and SOC2 evidence. Does Redwood Hosted provide customer-managed keys?
[00:02:55] Jordan: Hosted supports encryption at rest and in transit and we have a BYOK option for certain enterprise tiers; Dedicated adds isolation and can be configured with customer-managed KMS. For Private/on-prem you manage keys fully. We'll send the SOC2 deck and KMS notes after.
[00:03:10] Priya: From an infra point, for streaming the token emission rate matters. If your model emits at 20 tokens/sec vs 80 tokens/sec, that changes concurrency math. Do you have a token/sec distribution?
[00:03:22] Maya: We do not have precise distro yet; we can produce histograms. Our median is about 45 tokens per response and average token emission is about 30 tokens/sec — but like I said long tail exists.
[00:03:35] Priya: Okay good. For sizing, two quick back-of-envelope calcs: with 1.5k concurrent users at 30 tokens/sec each that's 45k tokens/sec sustained. With batching and GPU throughput you can get higher per-GPU token/sec, but streaming introduces per-token latency sensitivity.
[00:03:54] Liam: Can you explain the batching tradeoff again? We worry that batching increases latency even if it improves throughput.
[00:04:02] Priya: Right — batching amortizes kernel overhead and increases throughput but increases head-of-line latency. Redwood's continuous batching tries to adaptively group similar requests with small micro-batching windows to keep latency low while benefiting throughput. For initial chunk we keep micro-batch windows sub-10ms where possible, but at high qps you will see batching help overall cost.
[00:04:23] Carlos: What about KV cache? Our prompts often share prefixes — can caching reduce token compute?
[00:04:28] Priya: Absolutely. Prefix/KV cache can serve a lot of repeated context instantly. We call it KV cache, sometimes transcription spells it as K V cache, but yes that reduces compute per token dramatically if the continuing tokens are from cached prefixes. We will want your prompt set to evaluate hit rates.
[00:04:43] Sofia: On hosting decision, is Dedicated effectively guaranteeing GPUs to us?
[00:04:49] Jordan: Yes Dedicated is reserved pools for your account. SLA-backed throughput and lower tail variance. Hosted is multi-tenant with good SLAs but not the same isolation. Private gives you the most control — VPC peering, on-prem — but comes with ops overhead.
[00:05:03] Maya: For Private we'd need an air-gapped option? Some of our clients require no outbound traffic.
[00:05:09] Jordan: We have an on-prem package that supports air-gapped deployments; that often involves an enterprise engagement. We can outline what that looks like in the security doc.
[00:05:18] [00:05:22] Liam: Any real-world numbers you can share for p95 at different model sizes?
[00:05:26] Priya: From internal benchmarks — using a 13B-parameter model optimized for attention and kernel selection, we can hit 150-250ms p95 for initial token at moderate concurrency per GPU with micro-batching and prefix cache. Larger 70B variants push tails higher, often 300-600ms p95 depending on sequence length. These are approximate because the model architecture and quantization matter.
[00:05:48] Carlos: So if we pick a smaller quantized model, we lose quality — how do teams typically trade that?
[00:05:55] Priya: Typically you run parallel A/B evals — Redwood Optimize recommends quantization settings depending on workload. For assistant UIs, many teams accept 4-bit quantized 13B with little quality regression and huge cost/latency wins. We'll help instrument quality regressions tied to your eval prompts.
[00:06:12] Sofia: Does Redwood support tool-calling and function responses in streaming? We need structured partial outputs mid-stream.
[00:06:19] Jordan: Yes, streaming with structured tokens is supported; there's function-calling patterns and we can do chunked JSON patches. We'll demo that in the pilot if needed.
[00:06:28] Maya: About pilot — what's a realistic pilot run to validate p95 with our traffic?
[00:06:33] Priya: I'd propose a 48-72 hour benchmark window with your top 25 prompt templates, traffic replay at scaled concurrency (1x, 50%, 100% of expected). We'll run hosted baseline and a Dedicated run and provide token-level latency traces and p95 breakdowns.
[00:06:50] Carlos: Will Redwood provide the harness, or do we need to build it?
[00:06:54] Priya: We'll provide a harness — a small k6/journey-based runner and a reference harness for gRPC/HTTP streaming. We ask you to produce prompt sets, token histograms, and an authentication method (API key or temporary role) for the pilot.
[00:07:07] Liam: What about cold starts for KV caches and model warmup?
[00:07:11] Priya: There's warmup costs — we usually pre-warm model weights and cache expected prefixes. Cold starts can add a few hundred ms on first requests but are rare with steady traffic. Dedicated reduces cold start jitter.
[00:07:23] Carlos: For SLA, are there explicit p95 guarantees or just uptime?
[00:07:28] Jordan: Our Dedicated contracts can include throughput and latency SLOs for specific endpoints (negotiable). Hosted focuses more on availability SLAs. We can put latency SLOs into enterprise contracts for Dedicated customers.
[00:07:40] Sofia: How do you handle fallback during a capacity spike? Say we can't meet 200ms p95 for everyone — what's the graceful degradation path?
[00:07:48] Priya: We have automatic routing and fallback rules: degrade to smaller model variant, enable truncated responses, or route a percentage to a cached response. There are also circuit-breaker policies per route. We can show examples during the pilot.
[00:07:59] Maya: Do you provide token-level cost breakdown per model across Hosted vs Dedicated?
[00:08:04] Jordan: Yes the Console gives token-level cost + latency. We can share a sample breakdown and an estimated per-token unit-econ spreadsheet for your workload.
[00:08:12] Carlos: About network — VPC peering for Private, does Redwood support private peering to GCP?
[00:08:18] Jordan: We support VPC peering and private connectivity in Dedicated and Private deployments; specifics vary by cloud and region. We'll include the VPC peering checklist for GCP in the follow-up.
[00:08:28] Liam: Any security red flags we should expect in the docs? Our infosec will want SAML, RBAC, audit logs, and KMS integration.
[00:08:36] Jordan: Yes we'll include SSO/SAML integrations, RBAC, audit trails, and KMS/HSM notes. For Private/on-prem we hand the keys to you. We'll share SOC2 Type II report and ISO artifacts where allowed.
[00:08:49] Priya: Quick question for sizing — can you share expected QPS patterns across the day? Peaks and baseline?
[00:08:56] Maya: We'll send our 7-day profile. Peak concurrent is 1.5k, baseline usually 300-400, and we have bursts when marketing emails hit product.
[00:09:07] Priya: Perfect. That will help pick Dedicated pool size and autoscaling policies.
[00:09:13] Jordan: On the timeline — if the pilot looks good, do you expect to go Dedicated or Private?
[00:09:19] Carlos: We are inclined to Dedicated at first for rapid time-to-value and lower ops investment, but Private is on the table if infosec demands it. Decision dependent on pilot and cost.
[00:09:28] Sofia: Are there minimum commits for Dedicated?
[00:09:31] Jordan: There are reserved capacity contracts — monthly or annual commits. We'll send examples; some customers start with a smaller commit and scale up.
[00:09:39] [00:09:45] Maya: One more — how do you measure streaming p95? Is it initial token latency or full-stream tail?
[00:09:50] Priya: We report both. Streaming p95 initial chunk and p95 full emission time. For UX we often focus on initial chunk, which is most noticeable to users.
[00:09:59] Carlos: Great. Let's recap next steps.
[00:10:02] Jordan: Recap: we'll share SOC2/ISO + KMS and VPC checklist, Priya will provide a benchmark harness and instructions, Arkhaven provides prompt set and token histograms, and we'll schedule pilot week of 11/13. Anything else?
[00:10:14] Carlos: No, that's it. Thanks.
[00:10:17] Priya: Awesome, we'll follow up with the materials.
[00:10:20] Jordan: Thanks everyone.

(Transcript notes: occasional transcription mis-hearings: "kay-vee cache" for KV cache; "Redwood Dedicat" sometimes; speaker overlap near 00:06:30; filler words present.)

End of meeting.
